title: Rejoice always (Philippians 4:4–7)
hookLine: be nothing solicitous, and the peace of God keeps your hearts

cards: On one Sunday in Advent, a Catholic priest may set aside the purple and wear rose. On the wreath, the pink candle is lit.
That Sunday has a name, Gaudete, the Latin for rejoice, from the first word of the old entrance chant. And the chant is today's verse: Gaudete in Domino semper, rejoice in the Lord always.
The surprising part is where Paul was when he wrote it. Not on a holiday. In prison, not knowing whether he'd live or die.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice. Let your modesty be known to all men. The Lord is nigh." He says it twice, as if he expects them to hesitate.
Modesty here translates a Greek word that means something like gentleness or graciousness, not grabbing what's yours. Then: the Lord is nigh. Near.

teach.h: THE LORD IS NEAR: TIME, OR PLACE?
teach.b: Near in time, coming soon? Or near in space, right beside you? Readers have taken it both ways, and the verse can hold both.
Then comes the instruction: "Be nothing solicitous; but in every thing, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known to God."
Be nothing solicitous is an old way of saying don't be anxious about anything. And notice what Paul doesn't say. He doesn't say stop worrying because there's nothing to worry about.

teach.h: TURN THE WORRY INTO A REQUEST.
teach.b: He says take the worry and turn it into a request, with thanks attached. Then the promise: "And the peace of God, which surpasseth all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus."
The Greek for keep is a soldier's word: to guard, to garrison. Acts calls Philippi a colony: a piece of Rome set down in Macedonia.
Paul pictures God's peace standing guard at the gate of your heart. Not peace that understands everything.

teach.h: THE PEACE OF GOD, WHICH SURPASSETH ALL UNDERSTANDING.
teach.b: Peace that surpasses understanding: in Paul's words, it can hold even when the situation doesn't make sense. On Gaudete Sunday, the Church is still waiting for Christmas. The rejoicing comes before the gifts are open.

how: On the Third Sunday of Advent, Gaudete Sunday, Catholics light the rose candle on the Advent wreath, priests may wear rose vestments, and the entrance antiphon is taken from Philippians 4:4–5.

o: a carol sung only in the week of Christmas
a command to stay cheerful and never grieve
joy in the Lord that holds even in hard times

games.q: inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: near in time, or near beside you

s: Paul wrote 'rejoice always' during an easy time
he wrote from prison, not knowing if he would live.
Gaudete Sunday takes its name from Philippians 4:4
the entrance chant begins Gaudete in Domino semper.
Paul says to stop worrying because nothing is wrong
he says turn worries into prayer, with thanksgiving.

games.q: you're anxious about something you can't control. what does Paul tell the Philippians to do?
o: make it known to God, by prayer, with thanksgiving.
solve it alone before you pray.
games.why: "in every thing, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known to God." then peace stands guard.

practice: Let the loudest worry of the day come to the front, and name it plainly.
Instead of chewing on it, shape it into a request, help with this, watch over them, show me the next step, and set one thing you're thankful for right next to it.
If you pray, make it known to God just as it is; if not, set it down in words and notice whether anything loosens.

wordCard.voice: Rejoice always. Paul's words from prison, sung every Gaudete Sunday: rejoice in the Lord always, for the Lord is nigh. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: will guard, keep watch over, as a garrison does (Philippians 4:7).

carryVoice: Your line: the lord is nigh. Near in time, and near beside you. Until tomorrow.
